cards.heading: Three systems, not one
cards.hook: Node.js is three collaborating systems bolted together by its own C++ layer — V8 executes JavaScript and owns the microtask queue, libuv owns the event loop and all OS I/O, and neither one knows the other exists without Node's glue code in between.

cards.heading: Microtasks drain after every phase, not just once
cards.hook: Between every single libuv phase, Node flushes the entire process.nextTick queue and then the entire Promise microtask queue — this ordering is the one mental model that explains almost all async behavior in Node.js.

cards.heading: Your top-level code isn't inside the event loop
cards.hook: Every setTimeout, fs.readFile, and .listen() call in your module's top-level code just registers a handle during bootstrap — none of it has actually fired yet by the time the event loop starts turning.
cards.body: uv_run() is first called only after your entire module has already run synchronously once.

cards.heading: uv_loop_t is several structures, not one queue
cards.hook: There's no single unified task queue inside libuv — a timer min-heap, a pending-callback queue, an I/O watcher list, and a check-handle list are each drained by their own fixed phase of uv_run().

cards.heading: setTimeout(fn, 0) still has to wait its turn
cards.hook: A zero-delay setTimeout doesn't mean run immediately, it means insert into the timer heap at the current time — which still has to wait for the timers phase to come around in this or a future loop iteration.

cards.heading: An idle Node process isn't spinning, it's asleep
cards.hook: The poll phase computes a timeout and then genuinely blocks inside a kernel syscall — epoll_wait on Linux, kqueue on macOS — which is exactly why an idle server with nothing to do uses roughly zero percent CPU.

cards.heading: Why setImmediate beats setTimeout(fn, 0) inside I/O callbacks
cards.hook: Scheduled from inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always fires before setTimeout(fn, 0) in the same iteration, because poll just finished, check runs right after it, and timers don't run again until the next iteration.

cards.heading: One counter decides if your process exits
cards.hook: Every handle counts toward keeping the loop alive by default; calling .unref() on a timer or socket flips that single bit without canceling the handle, which is the entire mechanism behind why a script exits here but hangs there.
cards.code:
const timer = setInterval(() => {}, 1000);
timer.unref(); // fires, but never keeps the process alive alone

cards.heading: The drain happens after every callback, not every phase
cards.hook: A process.nextTick call inside one timer callback runs before the very next already-due timer callback in that same phase, because nextTick and microtasks drain after each individual JS callback, not just once at the phase boundary.

cards.heading: A recursive nextTick starves the loop completely
cards.hook: A function that keeps rescheduling itself with process.nextTick runs to completion and never lets libuv's phases proceed, because that drain happens before control is ever handed back to uv_run().

cards.heading: A worker thread isn't a callback on the main loop
cards.hook: A Worker is an entirely separate OS thread with its own Environment, its own V8 isolate, and its own independent uv_loop_t — it doesn't share the main thread's loop at all, which is why heavy synchronous JS in a worker never blocks the main thread.

cards.heading: cluster is not worker_threads with extra steps
cards.hook: cluster runs multiple fully separate processes, each with its own main() and its own everything, coordinated only by the primary process sharing the listening socket's file descriptor at the OS level.

cards.heading: Timer precision degrades under load
cards.hook: Node doesn't guarantee a timer fires at the exact millisecond requested, only that it won't fire early — if the loop is busy, timers consistently fire late, a pattern called timer drift.

cards.heading: process.nextTick outranks even Promise microtasks
cards.hook: nextTick has its own queue processed before the Promise microtask queue, which is a two-level priority system kept mostly for backward compatibility — in modern code, prefer promises over nextTick for async coordination.

cards.heading: Every socket and file handle eats into one OS limit
cards.hook: Default file descriptor limits are typically 1024 to 4096 per process, and running out produces the cryptic EMFILE or ENFILE errors — raise ulimit and systemd's LimitNOFILE before you hit it, not after.

cards.heading: Recursive setImmediate is cooperative multitasking
cards.hook: Breaking a long computation into chunks with recursive setImmediate calls lets I/O events interleave between chunks instead of starving the loop the way a single synchronous pass would.

cards.heading: I/O-heavy workloads can starve the loop too
cards.hook: If new I/O events keep arriving faster than their callbacks finish, the poll phase's queue never empties, and the loop never even reaches the timers or check phase — I/O starvation looks identical to CPU starvation from the outside.

cards.heading: Event loop lag is the health metric that matters
cards.hook: Lag is the gap between when a timer should fire and when it actually does — above 50 to 100 milliseconds is a real warning sign, and it should be on every production dashboard, not just checked when something's already wrong.

cards.heading: cluster doesn't give you sticky sessions for free
cards.hook: Round-robin connection distribution across cluster workers has no concept of routing the same client back to the same worker — that needs a reverse proxy doing IP hashing or cookie-based affinity in front of it.

cards.heading: Rolling restarts beat a hard restart
cards.hook: Stop one worker, wait for it to drain its in-flight connections, start its replacement, then move to the next — repeating this one worker at a time is what makes a cluster deploy zero-downtime instead of a brief outage.

cards.heading: Every async operation gets a number
cards.hook: A shared Float64Array holds the currently executing async ID and the ID that triggered it, backed directly by C++ memory, so JavaScript can read and write async tracking state with zero cost crossing the JS/C++ boundary.

cards.heading: The callbackTrampoline is the hot path for all I/O
cards.hook: Every TCP callback, file read, and DNS response gets funneled through one function that fires the before hook, runs the real callback, then fires the after hook — this single choke point is what makes async_hooks able to see everything.

cards.heading: A C++ stack tracks which async context is current
cards.hook: push_async_context and pop_async_context save and restore a stack of execution and trigger IDs in C++, so executionAsyncId() always reflects exactly which async operation is currently running, nested correctly however deep the chain goes.

cards.heading: async/await is Promises wearing a disguise
cards.hook: V8 compiles an async function into a state machine of chained .then() calls at compile time — the clean syntax doesn't add a new runtime mechanism, it's sugar over the exact same Promise machinery.
cards.code:
async function f() { const x = await g(); return x; }
// compiles roughly to: g().then(x => x)

cards.heading: Four lifecycle hooks mirror async_hooks exactly
cards.hook: init, before, after, and settled are the Promise-specific version of the same four lifecycle events async_hooks tracks for every other async resource, registered directly with V8.

cards.heading: Four distinct rejection events, not just one
cards.hook: V8's rejection callback distinguishes a genuinely unhandled rejection from a catch added late, from calling resolve or reject twice on an already-settled promise — each is a separate, trackable event, not a single generic failure.

cards.heading: A timer tick is six steps, not one callback
cards.hook: Exchange in the saved context frame, fire the before hook, run your callback, fire the after hook, restore the prior context frame, then flush nextTick and microtasks — every single setTimeout callback goes through all six steps.

cards.heading: Context across await needs an explicit snapshot
cards.hook: Without special handling, a value set with AsyncLocalStorage before an await would be lost by the time execution resumes — Node captures a snapshot of the current context frame when the async resource is created and restores it exactly when the callback fires.

cards.heading: Two implementations trade off overhead differently
cards.hook: AsyncLocalStorage has a lower-overhead path built on V8's native continuation-preserved embedder data, and a fallback path built on the async_hooks lifecycle — which one runs depends on whether the async-context-frame flag is enabled.

cards.heading: nextTick isn't a V8 microtask at all
cards.hook: process.nextTick has its own queue managed entirely by Node, separate from V8's microtask queue, and it always drains first — the real order is nextTick queue, then Promise microtask queue, then back to libuv.

cards.heading: Two completely different non-blocking mechanisms
cards.hook: True async I/O uses OS-level non-blocking calls that the kernel itself handles, while thread-pool async I/O just hands a blocking call to a background thread — fs, DNS, crypto, and compression all use the second, slower-feeling kind.

cards.heading: Only four threads back every fs call by default
cards.hook: If four file operations each take 100 milliseconds, a fifth one queues and waits the full 100 milliseconds before it even starts — thread pool saturation causes exactly this kind of lumpy, hard-to-explain latency.

cards.heading: Network I/O never touches the thread pool
cards.hook: TCP and UDP sockets use true async I/O via epoll or kqueue and scale to tens of thousands of connections on memory and file descriptors alone — file system operations are the pseudo-async one, limited by thread pool size and disk speed.

cards.heading: dns.lookup silently taxes your thread pool
cards.hook: Every unique hostname an HTTP client resolves with the default dns.lookup() consumes a thread pool slot via getaddrinfo — under load with many distinct hosts, DNS resolution alone can saturate the pool.

cards.heading: Neither DNS API caches by default
cards.hook: dns.lookup() and dns.resolve() both query fresh every single call with no built-in caching — implementing your own TTL-respecting cache is left entirely to you.

cards.heading: Atomic file writes need write-then-rename
cards.hook: A plain write to a config file can leave it corrupted if the process dies mid-write — writing to a temp file, fsyncing it, then renaming into place is atomic at the filesystem level and never leaves a half-written file behind.

cards.heading: Cluster mode multiplies your pool size by accident
cards.hook: Eight cluster workers each running a pool of twenty means up to 160 concurrent connections to the database, and most databases perform poorly with hundreds of concurrent connections — size the pool per worker, not per application.

cards.heading: Event emitters have no built-in backpressure
cards.hook: Unlike streams, an EventEmitter firing events faster than its listeners can process them just queues listener executions, which shows up as event loop lag and climbing memory with no backpressure signal to catch it.

cards.heading: Operational errors and programmer errors need different handling
cards.hook: A network failure should be retried, given a fallback, or surfaced to the user — a bug in your own logic should crash the process in development and get logged, never silently caught and ignored.

cards.heading: Three escape hatches for three different problems
cards.hook: Worker threads share memory and suit CPU-bound work, child processes are fully isolated and suit running external or untrusted programs, cluster mode is specifically for scaling network servers across cores — picking the wrong one wastes the hardware you're paying for.

cards.heading: Concurrency and parallelism are not the same thing
cards.hook: The event loop gives you concurrency, interleaved handling of many things at once on one thread — worker threads and child processes give you parallelism, actually running more than one thing at the exact same instant.

cards.heading: SharedArrayBuffer is the one true shared memory
cards.hook: Message passing between threads always serializes and clones data, but a SharedArrayBuffer lets multiple threads read and write the same memory concurrently — at the cost of needing Atomics for anything approaching thread safety.

cards.heading: Transferables move data without copying it
cards.hook: Passing an ArrayBuffer as a transferable hands ownership to the receiving thread with zero copy — the sender loses access entirely, which is the tradeoff for skipping serialization.

cards.heading: fork() is for talking to another Node process
cards.hook: Unlike spawn, exec, and execFile which run arbitrary commands, fork() specifically creates a new Node.js process wired up with its own IPC channel, designed for Node-to-Node communication.

cards.heading: The OS won't let two processes share a port directly
cards.hook: Cluster works around this by having the master process own the actual port and pass connections to workers over IPC, or on some platforms by sharing one socket reference across workers and letting the kernel pick which one gets each connection.

cards.heading: Workers don't share memory, so sessions break silently
cards.hook: A session stored in one worker's memory simply isn't there if the next request from that client lands on a different worker — the fix is an external store like Redis, not trying to pin clients to workers.

cards.heading: Restart crashed workers with backoff, not instantly
cards.hook: A worker that crashes immediately after starting and gets instantly restarted can spiral into a restart loop — throttling restarts with exponential backoff is what keeps a bad deploy from hammering the system.

cards.heading: Canary releases catch problems before they're global
cards.hook: Routing five percent of traffic to a new version first, then ten, twenty five, fifty if metrics stay healthy, catches a bad deploy while it only affects a small slice of users instead of everyone at once.

cards.heading: Most objects die young, so V8 optimizes for that
cards.hook: New space is small and collected constantly with a fast copying collector, old space is large and collected rarely with a slower mark-sweep-compact pass — this split exists because most objects are allocated, used briefly, and discarded almost immediately.

cards.heading: Buffers live outside the heap V8 is watching
cards.hook: A Buffer's backing store is allocated off the V8 heap entirely, so heap size limits and heap statistics don't account for it — a Buffer-heavy app can look fine on heapUsed while quietly running out of actual process memory.

cards.heading: Write barriers are the price of concurrent GC
cards.hook: Every pointer assignment pays a small extra cost so V8 can track changes during a concurrent marking pass — that overhead is what makes it possible to collect garbage on a background thread instead of pausing JavaScript entirely.

cards.heading: Scavenge pause time scales with live objects, not space size
cards.hook: A minor GC only touches objects that are still alive and copies them to the other semi-space — dead objects are simply never visited, which is why Scavenge stays fast even as new space fills up.

cards.heading: Incremental marking trades one long pause for many tiny ones
cards.hook: Instead of marking the whole old-space object graph in one stop-the-world pass, V8 interleaves small marking steps with regular JavaScript execution — individually barely noticeable, instead of one dramatic freeze.

cards.heading: A lost timer ID is a permanent leak
cards.hook: setInterval keeps its callback and everything that callback's closure captures alive in memory for as long as the interval runs — if you lose the reference to clear it, there is no other way to stop it.

cards.heading: Unbounded caches are leaks with extra steps
cards.hook: A cache with no eviction policy that keys on every unique input grows forever by definition — an LRU cap or a WeakMap for entries you don't need to keep alive turns a leak into a bounded cost.

cards.heading: Compare two snapshots, don't read just one
cards.hook: A single heap snapshot shows a lot of objects that look suspicious but may just be normal state — taking a baseline, performing the operation under suspicion, then taking a second snapshot and diffing constructor counts is what actually reveals a leak.

cards.heading: Container memory limits need headroom, not the whole box
cards.hook: Setting max-old-space-size to the container's full memory limit leaves nothing for off-heap buffers, the stack, and compiled code — on a 2GB container, 1.5GB for the heap with 500MB of headroom is the safer split.

cards.heading: Small buffer allocations share one pool
cards.hook: Buffers under 8KB are sliced from a shared pre-allocated pool rather than getting their own allocation each time, which cuts allocation overhead but means several small Buffer objects can silently reference the very same backing memory.

cards.heading: A settled promise's callback still runs later
cards.hook: Calling .then() on a promise that already resolved doesn't run the callback immediately — it's always scheduled as a microtask, which is exactly what keeps async timing consistent regardless of when a promise actually settles.

cards.heading: Promise.all starts everything immediately, not on await
cards.hook: All the promises passed to Promise.all were already running the moment they were created — Promise.all only controls when you collect the results, not when the work begins, so creating them in a loop and only then awaiting all of them is what actually gets you concurrency.

cards.heading: allSettled, race, and any solve three different problems
cards.hook: allSettled waits for everything regardless of failure, race settles with whichever promise finishes first and is the standard way to build a timeout, and any fulfills on the first success while only rejecting if every single one fails.

cards.heading: Concurrent batching bounds both throughput and resource use
cards.hook: Processing an array in chunks, running each chunk with Promise.all before moving to the next, gets you real concurrency within a chunk while still capping how many operations hit a downstream service at once.

cards.heading: A timeout doesn't cancel the operation underneath it
cards.hook: Racing a real operation against a timeout promise stops you from waiting on it, but the original operation keeps running regardless unless you explicitly cancel it with an AbortController — otherwise it just becomes wasted work finishing in the background.

cards.heading: Wrapping an already-promise-returning function in new Promise is redundant
cards.hook: If a function already returns a promise, use it directly — wrapping it in new Promise() just adds an unnecessary layer that complicates error handling for no benefit.

cards.heading: Sequential awaits silently throw away concurrency
cards.hook: Awaiting three independent operations one after another makes each one wait for the last to finish even though none of them depend on each other — creating all three promises first, then awaiting Promise.all, runs them side by side instead.

cards.heading: Streams exist so you never load it all into memory
cards.hook: fs.createReadStream processes a file chunk by chunk as it arrives instead of fs.readFile loading the entire thing into RAM first — for a multi-gigabyte file, that's the difference between working and crashing.

cards.heading: Stream state packs into a single integer
cards.hook: Instead of a dozen separate boolean properties, a readable stream's ended, flowing, and reading flags are each one bit inside a single 32-bit integer — cheaper to check, and it avoids creating differently-shaped objects that slow down V8's optimizer.

cards.heading: write() returning false is the entire backpressure contract
cards.hook: When a writable's internal buffer exceeds its highWaterMark, write() returns false — the producer is supposed to stop and wait for the drain event, and ignoring that return value is how streaming code quietly turns into an unbounded memory leak.
cards.code:
const ok = stream.write(chunk);
if (!ok) stream.once('drain', continueWriting);

cards.heading: highWaterMark default is smaller than you'd guess
cards.hook: The default high water mark is 16KB for a binary stream and just 16 items for an object-mode stream — tune it down for tighter memory control or up for fewer syscalls, depending on what you're optimizing for.

cards.heading: Node proactively prefetches into its buffer
cards.hook: A readable stream doesn't wait for you to ask before it reads — it keeps calling the underlying _read() as long as its buffer sits below highWaterMark, so data is usually already sitting there ready the moment you call .read().

cards.heading: A transform stream interlocks its two halves
cards.hook: The writable side can't accept the next chunk until the readable side has pulled the previous one out — when the readable side isn't ready, the writable's callback is parked and only fires again once a consumer calls read().

cards.heading: cork and uncork batch writes into one syscall
cards.hook: Corking a stream buffers every write call instead of sending each one immediately, and uncork flushes them all as a single batched write — useful anytime you're writing a header, body, and trailer that really belong together on the wire.

cards.heading: pipeline() cleans up every stream, not just the one that failed
cards.hook: If any stream in a pipeline errors, pipeline() destroys every other stream in the chain too — manually piping with .pipe() leaves you to wire that cleanup up yourself, which is why pipeline() is the one to reach for by default.

cards.heading: TLS is just another listener in the chain
cards.hook: The C++ stream layer uses a stack of listeners rather than a single hardcoded path — TLS inserts itself between the raw socket and the default listener, decrypting data before passing plaintext upward, with neither side needing to know the other exists.

cards.heading: Node streams and Web streams interoperate directly
cards.hook: ReadableStream.from() turns a Node Readable into a Web stream and Readable.fromWeb() goes the other direction, so the two ecosystems don't force you to pick one ahead of time.

cards.heading: fs.readFile is four syscalls wearing a trenchcoat
cards.hook: A single readFile call is actually a chain of open, fstat, one or more reads, then close — each step creates its own async request object and hands off to libuv, with the next step only starting once the previous one completes.

cards.heading: The synchronous UTF-8 path skips the JS state machine entirely
cards.hook: readFileSync with UTF-8 encoding calls straight into one C++ function that does open, stat, read, and close without ever touching the JavaScript-level request chain readFile uses — a genuine fast path, not just a blocking version of the same code.

cards.heading: fs.watch and fs.watchFile work completely differently
cards.hook: fs.watch uses real OS-level notifications like inotify or FSEvents and is efficient — fs.watchFile polls the file's stat on a timer, which works everywhere including network drives but burns cycles doing it.

cards.heading: Reads use different chunk sizes depending on what's known
cards.hook: When a file's size is known upfront, Node reads in chunks up to 512KB; when it isn't, pipes and some special files included, it falls back to reading in fixed 64KB chunks instead.

cards.heading: Even opening a file goes through the thread pool
cards.hook: Even the async fs API's first step, opening the file, dispatches to a libuv thread pool worker that makes the real blocking open() syscall — fs operations never get the kernel-native non-blocking treatment that sockets do.

cards.heading: Streams reuse the same read loop under the hood
cards.hook: createReadStream's _read implementation is just fs.read called repeatedly, pushing each chunk and signaling end of stream with push(null) exactly like any other custom Readable subclass would.

cards.heading: A dropped file descriptor reference is a real leak
cards.hook: Every open file consumes a file descriptor the OS limits per process — failing to close files, even ones that error out, leaks descriptors until EMFILE errors start appearing under load.

cards.heading: Default file creation mode is 0666 before umask
cards.hook: Files created by Node default to permission mode 0666, with the OS umask applied afterward to produce the final, usually more restrictive, permissions you actually see on disk.

cards.heading: The file extension decides which loader runs
cards.hook: .cjs is always CommonJS, .mjs is always ESM, and a plain .js file is decided by the nearest package.json's type field — defaulting to CommonJS if that field is absent entirely.

cards.heading: Every CJS file runs inside an invisible wrapper function
cards.hook: Your module's code never executes directly — it's wrapped in a function that injects exports, require, module, __filename, and __dirname as local variables, which is exactly why those five names are available without ever being declared.

cards.heading: Reassigning exports breaks the link to module.exports
cards.hook: exports starts out as just a reference to module.exports — assigning properties onto it works fine, but reassigning exports itself to a new object breaks that link silently, so the real replacement should always go through module.exports.

cards.heading: A module is cached before its code even runs
cards.hook: Module._load registers the new module in the cache before calling .load() on it, which is the entire trick behind circular requires — a second require() of a mid-execution file gets back its partial, still-building exports object instead of looping forever.
cards.code: Module._cache[filename] = module; // cached BEFORE module.load(filename) runs

cards.heading: require() walks up the directory tree for node_modules
cards.hook: A bare specifier like require('lodash') generates a list of candidate node_modules folders by walking upward from the requiring file's directory all the way to the filesystem root — which is exactly why a hoisted package in a monorepo's top-level node_modules is still found by files nested many folders deep.

cards.heading: Three caches make repeated requires nearly free
cards.hook: A relative-path fast-path cache, the main module cache keyed by absolute filename, and a resolution cache for the filesystem walk all work together — once warm, a repeated require() of the same file costs close to nothing.

cards.heading: ESM links the whole graph before any code runs
cards.hook: Parse, link, evaluate, and namespace are four strict phases — every import specifier in every module is resolved and the full dependency graph is built before a single line of actual module code executes, unlike CommonJS which resolves and runs each file in one shot.

cards.heading: Live bindings mean an export can change after import
cards.hook: An ESM named export is a live binding, not a snapshot taken at import time — if the exporting module later reassigns that value, every importer sees the new value immediately, which CommonJS's copied exports object simply can't do.

cards.heading: The exports field can block access to your own internals
cards.hook: Mapping a subpath to null in package.json's exports field makes importing it throw a package-path-not-exported error — the standard way a package prevents consumers from reaching into files it considers private.

cards.heading: Conditional exports pick a file based on how it's loaded
cards.hook: The same package specifier can resolve to a different file for import versus require, checked in object-key order against the conditions the current load style provides — this is how one package ships both an ESM and a CommonJS build without the consumer doing anything special.

cards.heading: ESM importing CommonJS relies on static pre-parsing
cards.hook: Named exports from a CommonJS file are only visible to an ESM import if they're statically detectable as enumerable properties — a module.exports object built dynamically in a loop at runtime won't produce named exports, only the default import, which always works.

cards.heading: require() of an ESM file works now, with one exception
cards.hook: As of recent Node versions, require() can load an ES module directly, synchronizing the async link and evaluate phases underneath — the one thing it still can't do is require() an ESM file that uses top-level await, since there's no way to synchronize across that.

cards.heading: The scheduling order is fixed and worth memorizing
cards.hook: nextTick callbacks run first and completely drain, then Promise microtasks drain completely, then the next libuv phase proceeds, and setImmediate specifically waits for the check phase after poll — mixing these up is a common source of surprising ordering bugs.

cards.heading: Objects with the same shape compile to faster code
cards.hook: V8 assigns every object a hidden class based on its property layout — when a function always receives objects shaped the same way, V8 generates a single optimized memory offset lookup instead of checking the object's shape every time.

cards.heading: Adding a property after construction can deoptimize a whole function
cards.hook: Initializing every property in the constructor, in the same order, with the same types every time, keeps an object monomorphic — adding properties afterward or deleting them changes its shape and can bounce V8 back from optimized machine code to plain bytecode.

cards.heading: allocUnsafe is faster because it skips zeroing memory
cards.hook: Buffer.allocUnsafe skips zeroing out the memory it hands you, which is faster but means it can contain old data from a previous allocation — never send one over the network before you've filled every byte yourself.

cards.heading: Headers use a null-prototype object on purpose
cards.hook: Incoming HTTP headers are stored on an object with no prototype chain at all, which both skips the lookup fallback to Object.prototype on every property access and prevents a header literally named constructor from colliding with an inherited one.

cards.heading: Cluster and worker threads solve opposite problems
cards.hook: Cluster gives you I/O parallelism across separate processes, each with its own event loop — worker threads give you CPU parallelism inside one process, sharing a module cache and starting faster than spinning up a whole new process would.

cards.heading: Transfer large buffers, don't copy them between threads
cards.hook: Passing a large ArrayBuffer as a plain message argument clones the whole thing — passing it as a transferable hands over ownership with zero copying, at the cost of the original buffer becoming unusable in the thread that sent it.

cards.heading: Event loop utilization near 1.0 means you're CPU-bound
cards.hook: eventLoopUtilization returns a ratio from 0 to 1 of how busy the loop has been — a value consistently near 1.0 means there's no idle time left to accept new work, and the fix is a worker thread or more processes, not a bigger instance.

cards.heading: Resolve hostnames once at startup, not on every request
cards.hook: A DNS lookup in a hot request path adds thread-pool contention and latency on every single call — resolving known hostnames once at startup and caching the IP avoids paying that cost per request.

cards.heading: Hundreds of requires at startup is a real cost
cards.hook: Each require() the first time pays for disk I/O, V8 compilation, and execution — a large dependency tree measurably slows down process startup specifically, which lazy-loading infrequently used modules can defer rather than eliminate.

cards.heading: CPU usage under 30% with limited throughput means I/O-bound
cards.hook: Low CPU utilization while throughput still plateaus points at an I/O bottleneck, not a CPU one — adding more cores to an I/O-bound service does nothing, since the bottleneck was never computation.

cards.heading: Why Node.js struggles with CPU-bound work specifically
cards.hook: A long-running synchronous computation blocks the single JS thread completely — every other concurrent request waits for it to finish, since concurrency collapses to sequential execution the moment the event loop itself is occupied.

cards.heading: Separate CPU-bound services from I/O-bound ones
cards.hook: Running an occasional image-processing or report-generation workload inside the same process as your I/O-bound API handlers means one slow computation can stall every other concurrent request — extracting it into its own worker pool or service keeps the two from fighting over the same thread.

cards.heading: Workload character can change with the time of day
cards.hook: A service that's I/O-bound during normal daytime traffic can become CPU-bound during a nightly batch job or month-end report run — monitoring continuously and adjusting resource allocation beats assuming one classification forever.

cards.heading: By the time Node sees a connection, the handshake is already done
cards.hook: The kernel completes the full TCP three-way handshake entirely in its own network stack — libuv's OnConnection callback only fires once a finished connection is already sitting in the accept queue waiting to be dequeued.

cards.heading: llhttp parses incrementally, not after the full request arrives
cards.hook: Headers can be parsed and delivered to your handler before the request body has even finished arriving on the wire — which is exactly why treating the request body as a stream, not a pre-buffered value, is the correct mental model.

cards.heading: Parser objects are pooled, not recreated per connection
cards.hook: Creating an HTTPParser instance has a real allocation cost, so Node keeps a free list of them — a closing connection returns its parser to the pool instead of discarding it, and the next connection reuses one instead of constructing fresh.

cards.heading: writeHead doesn't actually send anything yet
cards.hook: Calling writeHead only serializes the status line and headers into a buffer — nothing hits the socket until the first res.write() call, which is why you can still overwrite a header after calling writeHead as long as you haven't written body data yet.

cards.heading: No Content-Length means chunked encoding, automatically
cards.hook: If you never set Content-Length explicitly, Node switches to chunked transfer encoding and writes each write() call as its own length-prefixed chunk, because it has no way to know the total response size up front.

cards.heading: The ALB-vs-Node keep-alive mismatch behind sporadic 502s
cards.hook: If a load balancer's idle timeout is longer than Node's own keepAliveTimeout, Node can start closing a connection the load balancer still considers open and reuses — the fix is making sure Node's keep-alive timeout is always the longer of the two.

cards.heading: Ignoring write()'s false return defeats backpressure entirely
cards.hook: Node has no way to stop you from calling write() again after it returns false — a response generated faster than the client can receive it just keeps buffering in process memory unless you explicitly wait for the drain event, or use pipeline() which does it for you.

cards.heading: A server with zero request listeners just hangs forever
cards.hook: If nothing is listening for the request event, Node has no default response behavior at all — the connection sits open until it times out, which is why every bare http.createServer() example always registers a handler immediately.

cards.heading: HTTP/2 solves pipelining's ordering problem properly
cards.hook: HTTP/1.1 technically allows pipelining multiple requests without waiting for each response, but responses must still return in order — HTTP/2's multiplexed streams let many requests share one connection concurrently with no such ordering constraint at all.

cards.heading: Header names are case-insensitive, but Node normalizes them
cards.hook: HTTP header names are case-insensitive on the wire, so Node lower-cases every key in req.headers for you — rawHeaders keeps the original casing and order intact for the rare case you need the exact wire representation.

cards.heading: require('express') never touches the event loop
cards.hook: Resolving the module, reading it off disk, compiling it with V8, and executing it all happen synchronously during require — nothing about loading a module, however large the dependency tree, involves async I/O or the event loop at all.

cards.heading: app.get() is just pushing data onto an array
cards.hook: Calling app.get(path, handler) compiles the path into a regex and pushes a plain object onto the router's internal stack array — no sockets, no I/O, nothing async happens until a request actually arrives later.

cards.heading: app.listen() creates the handle that keeps the process alive
cards.hook: Underneath, app.listen() is exactly http.createServer(app).listen(port) — the resulting TCP handle is active and referenced by default, which is the entire reason a running server process never exits on its own.

cards.heading: A synchronous handler finishes inside one poll-phase callback
cards.hook: res.send('hello') with no await writes the complete response before control ever returns to uv_run() — the whole request, from bytes arriving to bytes leaving, happens inside a single I/O callback with the event loop never advancing to another phase in between.

cards.heading: An async route suspends and gives the loop back immediately
cards.hook: The moment an async handler hits await, it returns a pending promise and control unwinds all the way back to uv_run() — the event loop is completely free to serve other clients while that handler's database call is still in flight.

cards.heading: One slow client never blocks a fast one, as long as neither blocks the thread
cards.hook: While client A's handler is suspended waiting on a database query, client B's simple synchronous request can be fully parsed, routed, handled, and responded to in the gap — one thread, hopping between two unrelated pieces of work, never blocking on either.

cards.heading: A single blocking handler stalls every concurrent client
cards.hook: Replace an async database call with a synchronous CPU-bound computation and the same server that handled two clients concurrently now makes the second one wait for the first's entire computation to finish — there's no suspension point to hand control back to the loop.

cards.heading: Idle keep-alive sockets don't keep the process running, the listener does
cards.hook: Idle client connections eventually time out and close, removing their handles from the loop's active count — but the original listening socket from app.listen() never closes on its own, which is why the process runs forever until something explicit stops it.
